Wabash National Corp., a nationwide producer of semi-trailers and other commercial trucking equipment and headquartered in Lafayette, Indiana, will pay $50,000 and provide other relief to settle a pregnancy discrimination lawsuit filed by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), the agency announced.
The EEOC’s suit charged that Wabash National’s facility in Cadiz, Kentucky denied a pregnant employee’s accommodation request to transfer to a role that did not require lying on her stomach. Instead, the company forced the employee to take unpaid leave and ultimately gave her no choice but to return to her position as an assembler without modification.
Wabash National’s decision to deny the accommodation request caused the employee to fear for the health of her pregnancy, the EEOC said, and she was forced to resign at nearly eight months pregnant in November 2023.
The company also unlawfully required the employee to provide medical documentation and failed to accommodate her even though it could have provided changes similar to those the company provides for non-pregnant workers with similar limitations, according to the suit.
The alleged conduct violates the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, and the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended (ADA).

A Miami construction company owner has been charged with theft and workers’ compensation fraud after he allegedly underreported his firm’s payroll by almost $1 million, a deception that defrauded NorGuard Insurance of more than $100,000 in premiums.
Israel Carballo, head of Carballo Group LLC, was arrested Nov. 5, pleaded not guilty and was released on bond, court records show.
An investigator with the state Department of Financial Services found that in 2023 Carballo purchased workers’ comp coverage from NorGuard, a Berkshire Hathaway company. He claimed a relatively small number of workers, which kept his premium at about $9,300 for the policy year.
But the DFS investigator subpoenaed records from subcontractors that showed Carballo Group had actually paid some $1,074,000 to workers, the arrest affidavit attests. The investigation also found that Carballo had used check-cashing services to cash checks, presumably to pay workers in cash.
Had he correctly reported his company’s payroll, the annual premium would have been $109,863, the investigator said in the affidavit. Carballo has claimed indigent status, which could qualify him for a court-appointed attorney or public defender.
Florida Secretary of State corporation records show that Carballo Group was registered as a corporation in 2023 but was dissolved by the state agency after the company failed to file an annual report in 2025.

“I think he’s received a great deal of deference due to his alignment with the Republican Party and the tons of money he spent for the Republican Party,” Johnson said. “I have no qualms about examining his relationships to the state.”

Missouri to end state-run developmental disability case management
Some disability advocates worry eliminating state positions will remove a necessary layer of oversight of service providers
Support coordinators based in regional offices of the Missouri Department of Mental Health currently provide case management to more than 5,000 individuals with developmental disabilities, mostly in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
More than 5,000 Missourians with developmental disabilities who rely on state employees to help them access services will be assigned to outside agencies by the end of 2027, a move that will eliminate 299 state positions.
The Department of Mental Health’s Division of Developmental Disabilities currently provides direct case management to 5,152 people statewide. About 87% of Missourians eligible for services through the division already work with contracted case managers employed by nonprofits or county disability boards.
Support coordinators work with individuals with disabilities and their families to develop and monitor individualized support plans, which identify the person’s needs and goals and, with approval from the division, help them access services, including those funded through Medicaid.
Debra Walker, the department’s director of public affairs, told The Independent the change “will address caseload growth and focus (division) staff time on the division requirements of contract management, quality and compliance.”
The division has sought for years to shift support coordination to outside agencies as the number of Missourians eligible for services through the division has increased, citing the need to keep caseloads manageable. And the move is expected to save the state approximately $3 million annually, Walker said, as spending outpaces revenue and the pandemic-era surplus diminishes.
But some disability advocates worry the transition will disrupt services. Others are concerned that eliminating state-employed case managers could weaken oversight of organizations providing services to people with disabilities and make it more difficult for the state to follow federal rules barring individuals from receiving services from the same entity assessing their eligibility.
An Oct. 28 letter from the division obtained by The Independent tells clients to “continue to meet with your support coordinator as you usually would” and indicates they will be contacted by the division or their new case management provider once their case is transferred.
The transition, which will eliminate 299 state support coordination staff positions, including supervisors, is scheduled to be complete by Dec. 31, 2027.
Current employees will receive preference when applying for openings in the division’s regional offices, but none are guaranteed another position.
Walker said the division has already confirmed contractors’ capacity to serve clients who will be transferred from state support coordinators — 92% of whom are in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas.
Larry Opinsky, a disability advocate based in St. Louis County whose daughter uses self-directed services, said he isn’t worried about his family’s transition because he knows how to navigate the state’s disability service system. But for families less familiar with the system, he worries the transition could interrupt or delay services.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal.
But the Commerce Department is in charge "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."
The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.
Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate allies, resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday after admitting to an affair following scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly determined to be a Chinese spy.
Huang had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.
Asked if he believes Nvidia's highest-level processors have made it to China using the Singapore-based Megaspeed as a pass-through, Bessent said, "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down."
"The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," Bessent told CNBC. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"
"I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
Huang and Lutnick both have been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Thursday.
Eichamer, the Commerce spokeswoman, told CNBC on Friday that Lutnick "has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions."
Huang has separately been asked to sit for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 before the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs.
The Republican chairmen of those panels have also asked Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter to participate in a closed-door interview with them on Dec. 2.

Mike Clarke got his viral New York City Marathon moment, getting cheered on by none other than Ariana Grande herself, but his appearance in the November 1 race has now earned him a yearlong ban from New York Road Runners events.
The organization confirmed to Runner's World that Clarke used a counterfeit bib to enter the marathon, a violation of its Code of Conduct and Rules of Competition. NYRR said it learned about the incident through multiple sources and has barred him from competing in its races for the next year, although he has the opportunity to appeal.
"When individuals fraudulently enter our events, they jeopardize everyone's safety," a NYRR spokesperson said in a statement provided to Runner's World. "These acts are egregious and are antithetical to supporting the sport of running and its community."
According to reporting by the New York Post, Clarke wore a duplicate of a bib (No. 4207), which had been assigned to Nicolas Bourot, a French banking executive.
Bourot had spent a decade trying to secure entry into the NYC Marathon, and finally got his chance this year, finishing in 3:23:23—only to discover that another man appeared in race photos under his name and bib number. Fortunately, it didn’t affect Bourot's official finish time.
"It's not fair for all the runners," Bourot told the Post, noting how difficult it can be to earn a spot in the race.
Clarke's participation in the race attracted plenty of attention online, particularly after footage of him high-fiving the Grammy Award-winning artist near the finish line blew up on social media. One of his Instagram videos has surpassed 6 million views, while another is approaching half a million.
Clarke acknowledged to the Post that he wasn't officially registered, claiming the bib number held sentimental significance because of a friend who had died and that he didn't realize it had been assigned to another runner. When explaining the decision to participate anyway, he told the newspaper via text:
“At the end of the day they can call it unfair or cheating the system but for me it was to push my limits while running for this goal and have fun while doing it. [And] after [the] race, I received a medal but gave it to a kid afterwards haha!”

The bull market won't have it easy in 2027 as the vibes around AI investments weaken, Goldman Sachs warned.
"Although we expect solid AI investment growth to continue, our forecasts imply that the investment growth impulse — additional AI investment as a share of GDP — will peak in early 2027. From a macro perspective, this should be a manageable event. But it may be a bigger test for markets for three reasons," Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi said.
"First, the AI impulse has been a much larger contributor to growth in earnings and market value than to growth in GDP," Trivedi explained.
"Second, AI-related equities have taken credit for significant macro productivity gains, especially companies benefiting directly from the infrastructure boom, that have made them more vulnerable to any signs that we are on a less optimistic path," Trivedi added.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
"Third, the point at which growth rates peak (a "second derivative" turning point) often matters, even if underlying growth rates (the "first derivative") remain healthy. Moving through that peak allows markets to place limits on the upside of an uncertain distribution and, as growth decelerates, the period of positive surprises to expectations often ends too, as we may be starting to see for the AI capex cycle."
Stocks have already been put to the test entering the final weeks of the year.
Market volatility has spiked in recent weeks amid the midterm election aftermath, which will see Democrats take control of the House and Senate in 2027.
High-stakes earnings reports from hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) freaked out the market as they highlighted dwindling free cash flow.
The removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia (NVDA) CEO has also triggered a sharp sell-off in hot sectors.
At the same time, macro headwinds have intensified as crude oil prices remain elevated amid geopolitical friction in the Middle East, reigniting fears of sticky headline inflation.
Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said at Yahoo Finance Invest that he thinks the inflation problem is disturbing.
Trivedi added, "AI has contributed more to market gains than economic growth, so [it] is a bigger test for markets than the economy."

Twenty-five states and the District of Columbia allow abortions to be provided by health providers who are advanced practice clinicians, a category that includes physician associates, advanced practice registered nurses, nurse practitioners, certified midwives and certified nurse midwives.

It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app. It included eight one-minute intervals interspersed with one minute of recovery. The virtual coach of that run prescribed different speeds, including a mile pace which was “fast,” a 10K pace which was “faster, but slower than a mile pace,” and the slowest of the three, a marathon pace. No matter how much I tried, I couldn’t run at different paces. Over the course of my various flirtations, romances, and relationships with running, I’d always seemed to move at only two speeds: run and walk.
Disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds. The name? “Find Your Pace.” Excited about this fortuitous opportunity, I pressed download and started this short workout even though I had just struggled through the previous one.
Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace. Instead, he only referred to the Rate of Perceived Exertion, a metric that has been around for decades, but that I had, to be honest, ignored for all of that time. RPE is a purely subjective scale from 1 to 10. Typically, 1 refers to an effort level similar to sitting on your couch (i.e., no effort at all), and running at a 3 is a warmup effort. On the other end of the spectrum is 10, an all-out sprint, a pace you can’t sustain for more than half a minute.
Coach Cory explained that my effort level, or exertion, correlated to a variety of distances. For example, I should strive to run a 10K at an RPE of 6, a 5K at 7, and one mile at 9.
He also suggested that runners connect words to different effort levels—for example, the word “strong” when running at the RPE of 6. Honestly, though? At 6, I thought, This is hard, and at 7, I can’t do this. By the time I reached 9, I thought, I have to stop. Coach Cory, on the other hand, suggested I use the word “epic” to describe my fastest pace. He’s clearly an optimist.
These were very short intervals, so my breathing and heart rate didn’t rise much. But the difference I felt between this run and my previous runs was notable: I was pushing myself in a way I had never done before. I followed Coach Cory’s instructions back and forth on the same block, and not once did I look at my Fitbit or the app to see how fast I was going, which is what I was instructed to do during my previous runs. The whole exercise was over in 10 minutes. You may be thinking, Well, okay, but how fast were you? Did you actually run at different paces?
Turns out, yes, I did. Even more shocking, I had truly picked up speed during these intervals. My mile pace was 9:21, my 5K was 10:30, and my 10K was 10:54. Faster than I’ve ever run during a training run or race. During that one short workout, I realized I could create different paces based on my effort rather than trying to “find” different paces for each race distance.
I know that might seem like semantics, but the difference is meaningful. “Finding” something isn’t in your control, but “creating” is. When a training plan listed different goal paces, I couldn’t seem to reach them, but when I ran based on my RPE, I was able to distinguish between different efforts, and those effort levels translated to mile, 5K, and 10K paces.
This run was memorable. It gave me a boost to not give up on myself or my training.

Supercritical processing infuses the foam with gas under high pressure and temperature, then lets it expand in an autoclave—a machine that uses steam to superheat the environment. It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week plan.

3 Key Workouts to Go From Zero to Your First Half Marathon
Run/Walk
Run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).
Do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.
Continuous Easy Run
In week four of this plan, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.
Throughout the plan, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more important than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.
Speed Workout
The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.
You should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training plan, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.

Add in Strides
Short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your plan. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.

PEORIA, Ariz. -- In some Arizona Fall League seasons, there's a player who has that it factor. Ronald Acuña Jr. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Kevin McGonigle.
This year, it's Cardinals outfielder Tai Peete. Not only was he the developmental circuit's most electric player, he also was its Offensive Player of the Year. He slashed .351/.441/.662, set an AFL record by tripling in four consecutive games, topped the circuit with 20 steals and ranked in the top five in nine offensive categories. He also finished second in the Home Run Derby on Fall Stars Game weekend.

"Tai does it all," said Peoria Javelinas teammate Ike Irish (Orioles), who hits with Peete during the offseason. "He can steal, he can run, he can throw, he can bang. He's the real deal and he puts the work in. He grinds in the cages. He's perfecting his swing every day. So I'm not really shocked by this."
Peete's virtuoso performance in the Fall League caps an eventful year. A supplemental first-round pick by the Mariners in 2023, he switched organizations this February in a trade for Brendan Donovan. After never having to deal with any sort of serious injury, he sustained a concussion when he was tagged in the head in late May and then came down with an illness that sapped him of 25 pounds, sidelining him for six weeks.
When he returned, Peete -- the Cardinals' No. 17 prospect -- played the best ball of his career. He batted .339/.386/.614 with 10 homers and 11 steals in 39 games between High-A and Double-A, then tore up the Fall League.
Built like a wide receiver at 6-foot-2 and 193 pounds, Peete also features the well above-average speed befitting the position. He has exceptional bat speed, plus raw power and a strong arm that delivered fastballs up to 96 mph when he pitched at Trinity Christian HS in Sharpsburg, Ga. Age is also on his side, as he just turned 21 in August.
There never has been any question about Peete's tools and upside, but there have been some concerns about his bat. He hit .217 last year in High-A and carried a career 31 percent strikeout rate before he was sidelined in the middle of this season.
Peete cut his K rate to 23 percent in the final two months of Minor League play and 18 percent in the AFL. If he can make that kind of contact, he'll be a star.
Peete's swing-and-miss issues stem in large part from an extremely aggressive approach. Interestingly, he has fished for more pitches out of the zone than usual during his hot streak. His chase rate was 35 percent from July through September and 33 percent in Arizona, compared to 28 percent in his first three-plus seasons as a pro.
